data.interpretation: From period 5, orders fall. On-time delivery remains a goal, but the KPI now centres on neutrality: a road-use rule should not make any one company better or worse off than the others. No metric directly measures "gain or lose because of how the road is used". The closest are utility_gap (on-time deliveries minus sanctions, and sanctions come from road-rule violations), on_time_rate_gap and min_company_on_time_rate. The word "but" suggests fairness now outranks volume, though that is not certain. The KPI states no level for either goal, so no targets or guard values are set.

options.label: Fairness first: company utility gap as main goal

goals.text: Reduce the spread in utility (on-time deliveries minus sanctions) between the best-off and worst-off company
Watch the town-wide on-time rate so that delivery does not worsen
Watch the worst company's on-time rate so the gap is not closed by pulling the best company down
Watch total sanctions, since road-rule penalties feed into utility

options.note: Closest to "gain or lose because of how the road is used": utility includes the sanctions that road rules create, and this is the quantity that moved against C in D1. Utility is a count, so it also reflects how many orders each company receives, not only road rules.

options.label: Fairness first: on-time rate gap as main goal

goals.text: Reduce the spread between the highest and lowest company on-time rate
Watch the town-wide on-time rate so that delivery does not worsen
Watch the worst company's on-time rate so the gap is not closed by levelling down

options.note: Rates are normalised by each company's order volume, so differences in demand distort them less. Sanctions are ignored, though road-rule penalties are one way a company can lose because of road use.

options.label: Delivery first, fairness monitored

goals.text: Watch the spread in company utility so that no company is made relatively worse off
Watch the spread in company on-time rates
Watch the worst company's on-time rate

options.note: Keeps on-time delivery as the measure of improvement, using the rate rather than the count because order volume is falling. Fairness is only watched, not required, unless you supply a level for a guard.

concerns: The KPI is about the effect of road rules on each company, but the gap metrics measure differences in outcome from any cause, such as order volume, pickup locations or fleet placement. A change can shift a gap without being the cause, and a gap that exists without any rule change is not necessarily unfair.

Minimising a gap can be achieved by making the best-off company worse rather than the worst-off better. The options therefore watch min_company_on_time_rate. If you want a hard floor, please give a level; none is stated, so no guard value has been set.

"On-time delivery still matters, but..." can be read as fairness first (options 1 and 2) or delivery first with fairness as a constraint (option 3). The two can conflict: D1 raised town-wide on-time deliveries while lowering C's utility.

The previous KPI's concern that no company's customers wait badly (worst_company_p95_wait_s, against the 120 s promise) is not mentioned in the new KPI. Please confirm whether it should still be monitored.
With fewer orders, per-company rates and gaps rest on small counts and will vary more from seed to seed. Small measured changes in gap metrics may be noise.
The per-company vote already records which company gains or loses from a rule change. Adopting a change against a company's vote, as in D1, now directly conflicts with this KPI.

revisit.why: K1 read the old KPI as on-time deliveries (main goal), worst_company_p95_wait_s and unfinished. The new KPI makes company neutrality central, so the evaluation method and its watched metrics need to be re-chosen. The pending level for "badly" may no longer apply.

D1 adopted block_k 3 → 2 against B's and C's votes, and C's utility fell from 28.8 to 19.0. Under the new KPI, that is a company losing because of how the road is used. The justification also relied on peak-volume gains in on-time deliveries and waits, which may not hold in the quiet season. The change should be re-measured on utility_gap and on_time_rate_gap at the lower order volume.
